newsitem.title: NIGERIA: FEATURE - Nigeria turns prostitutes to evangelists.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Nigeria turns prostitutes to evangelists.

text.p: Prostitutes attracted to Nigeria's new federal capital Abuja may end up becoming evangelists instead.
The rapidly growing city has long attracted fortune hunters who take over the streets at dusk when other residents retire for the day.

Julie Useni, wife of Major-General Jeremiah Useni, the minister of the federal capital territory, thought there had to be other means of dealing with the influx of prostitutes and in 1995 set up the Daughters of Abraham Foundation (DAF) to "restore the dignity of women."
"The disgraceful sight of these call-girls on our streets motivated me to set up this centre which seeks to restore them to decent living," she told Reuters.
The Daughters of Abraham Foundation, which Useni she describes as religious-oriented, seeks to persuade prostitutes to quit street-walking in favour of virtuous vocations.
In addition to a vocational training unit, the foundation houses a "regeneration" section and a medical centre.
INFLUX OF PROSTITUTES A PROBLEM
The influx of the women of easy virtue has been a problem in Abuja for some time, as in many other urban areas of Nigeria.

During working hours, government offices are often thronged by troupes of women clad in revealing dresses -- who may be schoolgirls, workers or full time prostitutes, but all united in their mission "to grab our own share of the ill-gotten wealth of our patrons," as one of them put it.

At the Federal Secretariat where government ministries are based, officials found the presence of women "without clearly defined missions" so unsettling that a controversial directive was issued banning women dressed in mini-skirts, trousers and outfits considered indecent from government offices.
Many officials welcome the activities of the Daughters of Abraham Foundation, especially its regeneration arm.
"I think they are doing a decent job for the womenfolk," said social worker Cletus Ilomade.
STREET PERSUASION TO QUIT THE STREETS
Missionaries from the regeneration section go into the streets to persuade prostitutes to quit their trade for a place at the DAF.

"Through person-to-person and friendship evangelism, the prostitute is made to repent and give her life to Jesus," says Josephine Ekwunife, the missionary in charge of street persuasion at DAF. "Each converted prostitute is then followed up, counselled and established in the faith."

Subsequently, the convert is subjected to a thorough medical check-up and treated for sexually transmitted diseases. The medical centre also takes care of the medical needs of rape victims and teenage mothers.
Afterwards follows the vocational training phase, during which inmates are given training in catering, fashion design and other trades likely to lead to an independent livelihood.
TRAINING IS FOLLOWED BY MISSIONARY WORK THEN TRADE

At the end of their training, trainees are required to work for one year as instructors or missionaries, after which they are set up on their own with requisite equipment and take-off capital of 10,000 naira ($120).
"When I was first approached," recalls Angela Ajigo, a former prostitute and now a missionary at the DAF, "I abused the missionaries and threw away the pamphlet which they gave me.

"I later picked it up and took it home when I didn't get a customer that day. After reading the pamphlet, something told me to surrender my life to the centre for restoration; I thank God today I am happy with myself."
At present 20 former prostitutes are undergoing rehabilitation at the centre, while 25 have graduated in the last two years.
According to Useni, the centre's annual running costs are three million naira ($35,000) and she has so far been financing it herself with help from her husband and a few other individuals.
($1=85 naira)
